title: SQL Essential Training Chapter 4
description: Write and run SELECT queries with aliases, ORDER BY, and LIMIT against the WSDA Music database.

videos.title: Your First Query
videos.learning_objective: Write and run your first SELECT query to return a customer contact list
videos.discovery_objective: Open the Execute SQL tab, type the commented query SELECT FirstName, LastName, Email FROM Customer, run it with F5, and show the result pane with the contact list

exercise_artifact.description: WSDA Music Customer table with FirstName, LastName, Email.

choreography.target: the Customer table in the Database Structure tree

script_beats.text: In this video, we will write our first SELECT query to pull a clean customer contact list for WSDA Music management. The goal is to return only the columns we need from the Customer table, so the result is focused and immediately useful.

choreography.target: the result pane showing query output
the result pane showing query output
the comment block in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: The editor is empty and the result pane below it is blank. When we finish, the editor will hold a comment block followed by a formatted SELECT statement, and the result pane will show the customer contact list.

SELECT is the SQL command that chooses which columns to return, and FROM chooses which table holds those columns. Together they form the simplest useful query pattern: ask for specific data from one table. This keeps the result small and fast because the database does not waste time returning columns we do not need.

choreography.target: the comment block in the SQL editor
the SELECT clause in the SQL editor
the result pane showing query output

script_beats.text: The next three actions will add a comment header, the SELECT clause, and the FROM clause. Each piece will appear in the editor as it is typed, and the result pane will stay blank until we run the completed query.

choreography.target: the comment block in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: We type a comment header that records who created the query, when it was written, and what problem it solves.

segments.text:
/*
Created By: WSDA Student
Create Date: 2026-08-31
Description: Customer contact list for management
*/

choreography.target: the SELECT clause in the SQL editor
the SELECT clause in the SQL editor
the SELECT clause in the SQL editor
the SELECT clause in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: We type the SELECT clause, listing the columns FirstName, LastName, and Email. The interface updates to show the change.
We type FROM Customer to name the data source for the columns. The interface updates to show the change.

choreography.target: the SELECT clause in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: We run the query and the result pane fills with the contact list. The interface updates to show the change.

choreography.target: the Customer rows in the Browse Data grid

script_beats.text: We see 60 rows returned with FirstName, LastName, and Email for each customer, confirming the contact list is complete and the query ran exactly as intended.

action.detail: the Execute SQL tab shows a populated results grid below the query

choreography.target: the result pane showing query output
the Email column header in the result pane

script_beats.text: The result pane shows the complete customer contact list, with each customer record appearing exactly once in the order it is stored. Management now has a reliable set of first names, last names, and email addresses without extra columns cluttering the view. Because the database returned only the columns we requested, the output is compact and fast to scan.

choreography.target: the comment block in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: Adding a comment header at the top of the query is a professional habit. It records who created the query, when it was written, and what problem it solves, which helps anyone who opens the file later. Good comments turn a quick one-off query into documentation that the whole team can trust and maintain.

choreography.target: the comment block in the SQL editor
the finished SELECT statement in the SQL editor

script_beats.text: We have written our first SELECT query and pulled a complete customer contact list. The query returned only the columns we needed and included a clear comment header. Next, we will make those column headers friendlier for management reports by using aliases.

planned_queries: SELECT FirstName, LastName, Email FROM Customer;
